frase_gancho.texto: A stone jaguar with a secret carved into the hollow of its back.

puente_narrativo.texto: Move from the jaguar of the night to the eagle of the day: a young warrior whose face peers out from between the jaws of an eagle helmet, the uniform of the empire’s most feared soldiers.

guion_corto.texto: Before you, a stone jaguar crouches with its body tense, as if about to leap. It measures more than two meters long and almost one meter high. But what matters is on its back: a round hollow, about sixty centimeters wide. The Mexica called vessels like this one cuauhxicalli, «eagle vessel», and in them they placed the hearts of the sacrificed and other offerings for the Sun. The jaguar is no accident: it was the animal of the night and the underworld, and it was associated with rulers and sorcerers. It was found in December 1901, when the foundations of a house behind the Cathedral were being replaced.

guion_largo.texto:
This jaguar has a brother in stone: an eagle. It is also a cuauhxicalli, and it appeared in 1985, a short distance from where the jaguar was found. That suggests the Mexica conceived them as a pair. The eagle was the day and the rising Sun; the jaguar, the night and the Sun that crosses beneath the earth. It is the same duality as in the [Tamayo mural](mna_s00_mural_tamayo) you saw at the entrance, but carved in rock and with a very specific function.

There is a version of the myth of the Fifth Sun, recorded by Friar Bernardino de Sahagún, that explains why these two animals are so special. When the gods threw themselves into the fire to create the Sun, the eagle and the jaguar followed them. The eagle came out with scorched feathers, and the jaguar with black spots on its skin. That is why, the tradition says, the bravest warriors of Tenochtitlan were called eagle knights and jaguar knights.

Now think about the hollow in its back. On the inner wall, eagle feathers and jade beads were carved, symbols of what is precious. And at the bottom, two figures: Huitzilopochtli and Tezcatlipoca, two of the most feared gods, piercing their ears with maguey thorns. Like the king and the god on the [Teocalli](mna_s06_teocalli_guerra_sagrada) that you saw earlier, here too the powerful give their blood first. The underlying idea is very clear: the gods had given their blood to create the world, and people had to give it back.

The jaguar was much more than a wild beast. It was the animal that moves without a sound and sees in the dark, and for the Mexica it was the nahual par excellence, the animal alter ego of rulers and sages. It even had a god of its own, Tepeyóllotl, «heart of the mountain», a being with jaguar skin who was associated with caves, echoes, and tremors. When the earth roared, perhaps it was him. Its name, ocelotl, is also one of the twenty day signs of the ritual calendar, and its immediate neighbor is the eagle, cuauhtli. Look for them together when you reach the [Sun Stone](mna_s06_piedra_sol).

And there is another clue in the eagle. The last tlatoani, the one who defended Tenochtitlan in 1521, was named Cuauhtémoc, which is usually interpreted as «descending eagle», the Sun sinking toward the horizon. His name was almost an unintended prophecy.

Imagine it in color. Like almost all Mexica sculptures, it was painted: according to studies, the skin had an ochre tone with black spots, and the claws and the inside of the hollow were red, the color of blood and fire. Today you see it gray, but in its time it would have been very striking, almost alive.

Its discovery, in December 1901, was almost an accident. The house of the Marquis of Apartado was being rebuilt, at the corner of Argentina and Donceles streets, behind the Cathedral, when the jaguar appeared. No one yet knew that, a few steps from there and beneath the pavement, lay the Templo Mayor. Almost eight decades remained before the [Coyolxauhqui disk](mna_s06_coyolxauhqui) would appear, in 1978. Today’s city still hides much of yesterday’s.

texto.Material: Basalt with red, ochre and black pigments
texto.Origin: Historic Center, Mexico City (Marquis of Apartado house)
texto.Dimensions: 94 cm high x 120 cm wide x 225 cm long

texto.pregunta: Myth: A cuauhxicalli, «eagle vessel», could only be shaped like an eagle.
texto.respuesta: Reality: There were cuauhxicallis in the shape of eagles, of jaguars, and even cylindrical ones, like the Stone of Tízoc. «Eagle» alluded to the Sun and to warriors, not just to the animal.
